opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and they kind of compound on each other.

The first is just that the mental model most people have of AI risk is anchored on public deployment. When you think about a model causing harm, you picture someone using ChatGPT or an API to do something bad: misuse, jailbreaks, bioweapons uplift. That's where the visible incidents happen, so that's where attention, evals, and policy have gone. A lot of the frameworks, like the responsible scaling policies and much of the regulatory discussion, are triggered by the act of releasing a model to the world. Internal deployment sort of falls through the cracks because it doesn't look like "deployment" in the usual sense.

The second is visibility. Internal use is, almost by definition, not something outsiders can observe. Researchers outside the labs, journalists, and policymakers don't see which models are running inside a company, what permissions they have, or what they're being used for. It's hard to build a discourse around something you can't see. So even people who care about this have had relatively little concrete to point at.

Third, there's an intuition that internal use is inherently safer. It's your own employees, smart, careful people, so what could go wrong? That intuition made more sense when models were basically chat assistants. But it changes a lot once you have increasingly capable agents doing real work inside the company: writing code, running experiments, and touching the infrastructure the next model is trained on. At that point the internal setting is arguably where the highest-stakes deployment happens. The most capable model, often before it's been fully tested, gets the broadest access to the most sensitive systems, including the systems used to build and evaluate its successors. If you're worried about a misaligned model, that's exactly the place where it would have the most leverage, for example by subtly sabotaging safety research or influencing how the next generation is trained.

And finally, there's an incentive issue. Companies have strong reasons to use their best models internally as early as possible, especially for accelerating AI R&D, because that's a competitive advantage. There's not much external pressure pushing back, because nobody outside is watching. So you get a situation where the risk is plausibly growing fastest in the place with the least oversight.

So my overall take is that it's less that people considered it and decided it was unimportant, and more that it didn't fit the existing frame. I think that's starting to change, but the field is still pretty far behind where it should be given how much AI companies are going to rely on their own systems over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response says outsiders cannot see which models run internally, their permissions, or their uses, but it does not identify limited understanding of internal development processes as a reason for the lack of attention.

r002.rationale: It describes an intuition that employee use is safer and says that intuition fit when models were chat assistants. It does not say staff dismiss risks because historically harmless models shaped their experience.

r003.rationale: The response describes risks arising inside a company, including sabotage of safety research, but does not observe that taking those risks seriously requires acknowledging they could arise within one’s own company.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there are a few things going on, and they compound each other.

The first is just that external deployment is where the public interface is. When a model gets released through an API or a chat product, that's the moment journalists write about it, that's the moment regulators can point to something concrete, that's the moment users notice behaviour they don't like. Internal use has none of that. If a lab is running its newest model on its own research cluster to accelerate its own work, nobody outside sees it, and so there's no natural trigger for anyone to pay attention.

The second is that a lot of the governance machinery that's been built over the past few years is implicitly keyed to the release moment. Responsible scaling policies, preparedness frameworks, the pre-deployment testing agreements with government institutes — almost all of that is framed around "before we deploy this externally, we do X." And that framing made sense historically, because the main worry was misuse by outside actors. But it means that internal deployment often sits in a kind of blind spot, where you might have a model that's been internally in heavy use for months before any of those commitments formally kick in.

The third thing, and I think this is the one that's most important, is that people underestimate how different the situation is once models are actually useful for AI R&D itself. If you have a system that can meaningfully speed up your own research, the incentive is to use it as much as possible, as early as possible, with as few restrictions as possible, because that's where the competitive advantage comes from. And the people deciding how much to restrict it are the same people who benefit from not restricting it. So you've got the strongest capabilities, the weakest external oversight, and the strongest incentive to cut corners all in the same place.

And then on top of that, the threat models that matter most for internal deployment are the ones that are hardest to make vivid. With external deployment you can say "someone might use this to make a bioweapon," and people get it. With internal deployment, the worry is more like: a model that's subtly misaligned gets used to write the next generation of training code, or to do the safety research on itself, or has broad access to internal systems and weights, and we don't have good ways of checking whether it's doing what we think it's doing. That's a much more abstract story. It requires you to already take scheming or sabotage seriously as a possibility, and a lot of people in the policy world haven't fully internalised that yet.

So I'd say it's a combination of visibility, the way existing commitments were scoped, misaligned incentives inside the labs, and the fact that the scary scenarios here are genuinely harder to explain. My worry is that by the time it becomes obviously important, we'll already be in the regime where a lot of frontier research is being done by models that nobody has properly evaluated for that use.

r001.rationale: The response says internal use is invisible to outsiders, but does not identify outsiders’ limited understanding of companies’ internal development and deployment processes as the reason.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss staff generalizing from historically harmless models or dismissing risks on that basis.

r003.rationale: The response describes risks and incentives within labs, but does not say that taking those risks seriously requires acknowledging they could arise within one’s own company.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that people tend to picture deployment as releasing a model to the public. You train it, you evaluate it, and then you decide whether users should have access. Internal use feels like something that happens before the real deployment decision, even though it can involve giving the model access to very sensitive things.

If you use an AI system to help develop the next generation of AI, it might have access to your code, your experiments, and information about how you evaluate models. So the relevant question isn’t just, “Have we released this?” It’s, “What can the system actually do, and how well can we tell whether it’s doing what we intended?” An internal system could have much more consequential access than the version available to the public.

There’s also a visibility issue. Outsiders can study a public product. They generally can’t see how a company uses models internally, so it’s harder to build a concrete discussion around those risks.

And I think there’s an understandable intuition that, because the people using it internally are experts and aren’t deliberately trying to cause harm, the situation is relatively safe. That does help with some risks. But it doesn’t resolve the possibility that the model itself behaves in an unintended way, or that people give it more responsibility than they can effectively oversee.

r001.rationale: It says outsiders generally cannot see how a company uses models internally, making it harder to discuss those risks concretely.

r002.rationale: It mentions the intuition that expert staff are unlikely to cause harm, but does not connect that intuition to historically harmless models.

r003.rationale: It discusses risks from internal systems generally, but does not say that taking them seriously requires recognizing they could arise within one’s own company.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that the most visible risks are about what happens when you release a model to the public. People can interact with it, discover dangerous capabilities, and ask whether it might help someone carry out a cyberattack or develop a biological weapon. Internal deployment is much harder to see from the outside, so it’s harder to scrutinise.

But there’s also a framing issue. It’s natural to think of the company as the entity controlling the AI, and therefore to assume that using it inside the company is relatively safe. That assumption becomes less reliable as you give systems more autonomy, access to sensitive information, and opportunities to act without a human checking every step.

For example, if you use an AI to help with AI research, you might be giving it access to code, experimental results, and parts of the process that determines what the next model looks like. Then the question isn’t just whether an outside user can misuse it. It’s whether you can reliably understand and oversee what it’s doing in that environment.

And there are strong incentives to use these systems internally: that’s potentially a huge source of productivity and competitive advantage. So I think we need to treat internal deployment as a consequential deployment decision in its own right, with evaluations and safeguards appropriate to the access and autonomy the system actually has.

r001.rationale: The response says internal deployment is harder to see from outside and therefore harder to scrutinise, capturing outsiders’ limited visibility into internal processes.

r002.rationale: It does not mention historically harmless models or staff becoming dismissive because of that experience.

r003.rationale: It challenges the assumption that a company’s control makes internal AI use relatively safe and describes risks in the company’s own internal environment.
